Computing the ACWR on a daily calendar

Source: vignettes/daily-calendar.Rmd
daily-calendar.Rmd
library(ACWR)

Since version 0.2.0, every method in ACWR works on a daily calendar. Each athlete’s sessions are placed on a series of days from the first to the last date: sessions on the same day are summed, and days without a session count as a load of 0. This vignette shows what that means in practice.

The data

training_load_rest holds the simulated training load of three athletes over eight weeks, with rest days:

data("training_load_rest", package = "ACWR")
head(training_load_rest)
#>   ID Week Day  TL Training_Date
#> 1  1    1   1 439    2022-01-03
#> 2  1    1   2 419    2022-01-04
#> 3  1    1   4 396    2022-01-06
#> 4  1    1   6 391    2022-01-08
#> 5  1    2   8 446    2022-01-10
#> 6  1    2   9 452    2022-01-11

# Sessions per week
table(ID = training_load_rest$ID, Week = training_load_rest$Week)
#>    Week
#> ID  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
#>   1 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4
#>   2 6 6 6 6 0 6 6 6
#>   3 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 6

Athlete 1 trains 4 days a week. Athlete 2 trains 5 days a week with a double session on Wednesdays (6 sessions) and does not train in week 5. Athlete 3 trains 3 days a week and 6 days in the last week.

The three methods

For each day t, with w the daily load:

  • RAC (coupled): acute = sum of w over days t-6 to t; chronic = sum over days t-27 to t, divided by 4.
  • RAU (uncoupled): same acute load; chronic = sum over days t-27 to t-7, divided by 3.
  • EWMA: Et = wt λ + (1 - λ) Et-1, with λ = 2 / (N + 1), N = 7 (acute) and 28 (chronic), updated every calendar day including rest days (Williams et al., 2017).

RAC and RAU acute and chronic loads are weekly-equivalent sums, so they read as “load per week”. ACWR() computes all three for every athlete and returns one row per session, in the original order:

res <- ACWR(db = training_load_rest,
            ID = "ID",
            TL = "TL",
            days = "Day",
            training_dates = "Training_Date",
            ACWR_method = c("EWMA", "RAC", "RAU"))

# Last session of each athlete
last <- res[!duplicated(res$ID, fromLast = TRUE),
            c("ID", "Training_Date", "EWMA_ACWR", "RAC_ACWR", "RAU_ACWR")]
format(last, digits = 3)
#>     ID Training_Date EWMA_ACWR RAC_ACWR RAU_ACWR
#> 32   1    2022-02-26      1.01    0.939     0.92
#> 74   2    2022-02-26      1.12    1.259     1.38
#> 101  3    2022-02-26      1.53    1.698     2.21

Athlete 3, who doubled the number of sessions in the last week, shows the highest ratios.

What changes versus 0.1.0

Version 0.1.0 averaged the load per session inside each window and decayed EWMA once per session, ignoring the dates. Results were only correct when there was exactly one session every day.

Take an athlete who trains 3 days a week (500 AU per session) for four weeks and then 6 days in week 5. The weekly load doubles, from 1500 to 3000 AU, but the load per session stays at 500 AU:

day <- c(0, 2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28:33)
dates <- as.Date("2024-01-01") + day
load <- rep(500, length(day))

rac <- RAC(TL = load, training_dates = dates)
rau <- RAU(TL = load, training_dates = dates)
ewma <- EWMA(TL = load, training_dates = dates)

# Ignoring the dates reproduces the per-session EWMA of 0.1.0
ewma_sessions <- suppressMessages(EWMA(TL = load))

n <- length(load)
data.frame(
  method = c("RAC", "RAU", "EWMA"),
  version_0.1.0 = c(1.00, 1.86, round(ewma_sessions$EWMA_ACWR[n], 2)),
  version_0.2.0 = round(c(rac$RAC_ACWR[n], rau$RAU_ACWR[n],
                          ewma$EWMA_ACWR[n]), 2)
)
#>   method version_0.1.0 version_0.2.0
#> 1    RAC          1.00          1.60
#> 2    RAU          1.86          2.00
#> 3   EWMA          1.00          1.33

The RAC and RAU values of 0.1.0 are quoted from NEWS.md, as that code is no longer in the package. With per-session averages, doubling the number of sessions is invisible: the coupled ratio stays at 1. On the daily calendar the acute week is 3000 AU and the coupled chronic load 1875 AU per week, a ratio of 1.6.

Warm-up period and partial = TRUE

RAC and RAU need 28 days of history, so by default they are NA until then:

a1 <- training_load_rest[training_load_rest$ID == 1, ]
rac_default <- RAC(TL = a1$TL, training_dates = a1$Training_Date)
rac_partial <- RAC(TL = a1$TL, training_dates = a1$Training_Date,
                   partial = TRUE)

data.frame(day = a1$Day,
           default = round(rac_default$RAC_ACWR, 2),
           partial = round(rac_partial$RAC_ACWR, 2))[c(1:3, 15:18), ]
#>    day default partial
#> 1    1      NA    1.00
#> 2    2      NA    1.00
#> 3    4      NA    1.00
#> 15  25      NA    0.92
#> 16  27      NA    0.92
#> 17  29    0.92    0.92
#> 18  30    0.92    0.92

With partial = TRUE, the days available are used and rescaled to 7 days (sum x 7 / number of days). This is a choice of the package, not of the cited sources, and early values rest on very few days: interpret them with care.

Limitations of the ACWR

The package calculates the ACWR as it is described in the literature, but the ratio has well-documented limitations:

  • Mathematical coupling. In the coupled ratio, the acute week is also part of the chronic load, which creates a spurious correlation between the two and reduces the between-athlete variability of the chronic load (Lolli et al., 2019); the coupled ratio can never exceed 4 (Windt & Gabbett, 2019).
  • Ratio artefacts. The ACWR behaves as a rescaling of the acute load, and adds no predictive value over the acute load alone (Impellizzeri et al., 2021). EWMA values depend on the initial load in the first weeks (Wang et al., 2020).
  • No validated thresholds. Recommended thresholds (e.g. a “sweet spot” of 0.8-1.3) are affected by these limitations and should not be used as cut-offs for injury risk (Wang et al., 2020; Impellizzeri et al., 2021).

References

  • Impellizzeri FM, Woodcock S, Coutts AJ, et al. (2021). What role do chronic workloads play in the acute to chronic workload ratio? Time to dismiss ACWR and its underlying theory. Sports Medicine, 51(3), 581-592. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01378-6
  • Lolli L, Batterham AM, Hawkins R, et al. (2019). Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 53(15), 921-922. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098110
  • Wang C, Vargas JT, Stokes T, et al. (2020). Analyzing activity and injury: lessons learned from the acute:chronic workload ratio. Sports Medicine, 50(7), 1243-1254. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01280-1
  • Williams S, West S, Cross MJ, Stokes KA (2017). Better way to determine the acute:chronic workload ratio? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(3), 209-210. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096589
  • Windt J, Gabbett TJ (2019). Is it all for naught? What does mathematical coupling mean for acute:chronic workload ratios? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 53(16), 988-990. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098925
